title: Battle of Outpost Betty (1953): 34 Men vs a Full Battalion
subtitle: July 15 – 16, 1953

lines: The night of July 15th, 1953. North of the Imjin River, in Yeoncheon, Korea.
Just twelve days remained before the guns would fall silent.
s01.label: Dramatization

lines: On a small hill across the river, Outpost Betty, a single South Korean platoon held on.
And in the darkness, Chinese troops were crawling up its slopes.
s02.label: Dramatization

lines: Thirty-four South Korean soldiers, against a Chinese force of battalion strength.
Their platoon leader, Kim Man-sul, decided he would not abandon the position.
callouts: ROK records: 2 Chinese battalions · platoon size 34–36 by source

lines: A night-long grenade battle, and shells called down on their own heads.
When dawn came, South Korean soldiers were still standing on the hill.
s04.text:
A night of blood,
and at dawn the hill was

lines: One last stand for a sliver of ground, on the eve of the armistice.
This is the story of the Battle of Outpost Betty.
s05.title: Outpost Betty

lines: By the summer of 1953, two years of armistice talks were nearing their end.
Both sides launched final attacks across the front, fighting for every last foot of ground.
For nearly two years, the front had barely moved.
All along the line, hills changed hands again and again.
s06b.label: Shell-torn ground around Outpost Boulder City (Jul 1953)

lines: On July 13th, the Chinese launched a massive offensive around Kumsong on the central front.
At the same time, attacks hit outposts across the western front as well.
In Yeoncheon, held by the ROK 1st Division, the Imjin River makes a great bend.
Across the river from the main line, a lone outpost hill jutted out.
callouts: ROK 1st Division sector · Imjin River bend

lines: Betty stood about one kilometer forward of the main line, an eye watching the enemy.
Lose it, and the positions south of the river would lie exposed.
callouts: ~1 KM FORWARD OF THE MAIN LINE

lines: It was barely over a hundred meters high, but steep on every side.
Chinese positions in front, the Imjin behind. There was nowhere to fall back.
s09.title: Outpost Betty · Terrain Profile

lines: It was held by 2nd Platoon, 6th Company, 2nd Battalion, 11th Regiment, ROK 1st Division.
Its leader, Kim Man-sul, had enlisted in 1947 and fought from Tabu-dong to Pyongyang.
s10.label: Kim Man-sul (1929–1991)

lines: Just a day before the battle, he passed his battlefield commissioning exam.
So Korean records list him as a second lieutenant, and U.S. records as a master sergeant.
Whatever his rank, that night he was the leader of this small platoon.
On the evening of July 15th, he led his men up Betty and took over the position.
A small platoon, recorded as 34, 35, or 36 men depending on the source.
s12.label: ROK platoon leader briefs his platoon sergeant, 9th Div (May 1953)

lines: That night, the shelling began.
Chinese artillery and mortar rounds rained down on the tiny hilltop.
s13.label: Dramatization

lines: Trenches caved in, and the phone line to the rear was cut.
In an instant, the hill became an island across the river.
s14.label: ROK Capital Div. soldier wounded in the Chinese July offensive (Jul 15, 1953)

lines: Then Chinese infantry began climbing the slopes from several directions.
U.S. records say a battalion; Korean records say two battalions.
Blowing bugles and whistles, the Chinese surged forward in the dark.
Every time a flare burst, the slopes were full of shadows.
s15b.label: Dramatization

lines: As the enemy reached the edge of the trenches, a grenade battle broke out.
Grenades flew back and forth at a distance where faces could be seen.
s16.label: Dramatization

lines: Kim ran along the trench line, throwing grenades himself.
His U.S. award citation records that his grenades killed six of the enemy.
s17.label: Dramatization

lines: It states that he fought the enemy hand to hand through the night and stopped the position from being overrun.
s17b.label: 9th ROK Div. soldiers wounded fighting the Chinese, White Horse (Oct 1952)

lines: The enemy pulled back, then came again.
The attacks went on all night, five to nineteen times, depending on the record.
s18.text: They fell back, and came again

lines: To restore communications, Staff Sergeant Lee Kang-ro reportedly ran through the shellfire to headquarters.
In trenches out of ammunition, men fought with bayonets and rifle butts.
s19.label: Wounded ROK soldier carried through a trench, Capital Hill (Sep 1952)

lines: One by one, the platoon's men fell.
The survivors gathered the ammunition of the fallen and took their places again.
Still, Kim would not give up the hill.
s20.label: Dramatization

lines: As dawn approached, the enemy finally broke into the trenches.
Kim seized the radio and made an almost unthinkable request.
s21.label: Dramatization

lines: He asked his own artillery to drop shells right on top of his position.
Fire on a hill where friend and foe were tangled together: fire on his own lines.
s22.sub: Artillery called onto your own lines when the enemy breaks in

lines: Shells bursting overhead could kill his own men too.
Even so, he chose that risk over losing the hill.
s22b.label: ROK artilleryman checks aiming data, 2nd Div (Feb 1953)

lines: The soldiers pressed themselves flat at the bottom of their trenches.
Above them, friendly shells swept the Chinese off the slopes and the hilltop.
s23.title: Fire on Our Position

lines: When the barrage lifted, the survivors charged out of their trenches.
They drove the remaining enemy back down the slopes.
As dawn broke, Outpost Betty was once again in South Korean hands.
s24.label: Dramatization

lines: Morning, July 16th.
The night-long battle was over.
A few exhausted soldiers stood on the hill.
Their uniforms were caked with blood and dirt.
Of the 34, only about twelve, including their leader, are said to have survived.
s26.label: Dramatization

lines: Korean records count 314 Chinese killed and an estimated 450 wounded.
Numbers hard to believe for a single platoon.
s27.note: Per ROK records · friendly losses vary by source

lines: Eleven days later, on July 27th, the armistice was signed.
Betty ended up inside the Demilitarized Zone, between North and South.
The ground they held to the last moment remains there to this day.
s28.label: Signing of the Korean Armistice, Panmunjom (Jul 27, 1953)

lines: How could one platoon hold off a battalion-size force all night?
Let's break it down into four factors.
s29.head: 34 Men vs a Battalion — How?

lines: First, steep ground.
s30.title: Steep Ground

lines: The enemy had to climb steep slopes, on a narrow front.
The terrain kept large numbers from attacking at once.
And with the Imjin at their backs, there was no road of retreat.
s31.title: A Narrow Front

lines: Second, the grenade fight.
s32.title: The Grenade Fight

lines: In darkness and on steep slopes, the grenade was the deadliest weapon.
The side throwing downhill had the clear advantage.
s33.label: Dramatization

lines: Third, fire on his own position.
s34.title: Fire on Own Position

lines: The men flat in their trenches survived, while the enemy in the open took the full blast.
Making himself the target was the decision that won the hill back.
Fourth, a leader who stayed.
s36.title: A Leader Who Stayed

lines: Kim led his platoon from the most dangerous spot, throwing grenades himself.
He was first to grab a grenade, and last to leave the trench.
That is what kept even the last few men fighting.
s37.label: Dramatization

lines: For this battle, Kim received Korea's Taeguk Order of Military Merit and the U.S. Distinguished Service Cross.
The DSC is the U.S. Army's highest award for valor after the Medal of Honor.
s38.sub: For the Battle of Outpost Betty

lines: In 1956, a film about his story, 'Repulse,' was even made.
A bust of him still stands in Paju's Unification Park.
s38b.label: Taeguk Order of Military Merit

lines: U.S. Army General Orders No. 35, dated May 13th, 1954.
On the citation, his name is written as 'Man Soul Kim.'
s39.head: DSC CITATION
s39.note: Summary of U.S. Army citation · reconstructed

lines: After the war, a training accident in 1958 left him paralyzed from the waist down.
Retiring as a captain, he founded a school and cared for disabled veterans.
s40.label: Korean War memorial statue, Yeoncheon

lines: In 1991, his wartime wounds flared up again, and he passed away.
Today he rests in Seoul National Cemetery.
s41.label: Seoul National Cemetery

lines: Today, from the Taepung Observatory in Yeoncheon, you can see Outpost Betty across the Imjin, inside the DMZ.
So close you could almost touch it, yet still a place no one can enter.
s42.label: The Imjin River along the DMZ (2012)

lines: Thirty-four men, and one night.
On that night, less than two weeks before the armistice, what they held was a sliver of their country.
quotes: A sliver of ground, held to the end
